we present a suite of scheming reasoning evaluations measuring two types of reasoning capabilities that we believe are prerequisites for successful scheming

we demonstrate how these evaluations can be used as part of a scheming inability safety case: a model that does not succeed on these evaluations is almost certainly incapable of causing severe harm via scheming in real deployment
Evaluating Frontier Models for Stealth and Situational Awareness
Mary Phuong*,1 , Roland S. Zimmermann*,1 , Ziyue Wang*,1 , David Lindner1 , Victoria Krakovna1 , Sarah Cogan1 , Allan Dafoe1 , Lewis Ho1 and Rohin Shah1
Submitted on 2 May 2025 ( v1 ), last revised 3 Jul 2025 (this version, v4)
we argue that two capabilities are necessary for a misaligned model to cause harm via our threat models: situational awareness and stealth ability
we think of situational awareness as consisting of three key components
our evaluations focus on agentic settings with scope for exploration and self-reasoning (and do not directly test for the knowledge component)
the agent is equipped with standard tools and has edit access to various files including its own source code and config
crucially, neither the (simulated) deployment setup nor the constraint is explained to the model
we present a suite of eleven such situational awareness challenges
all but two of our proposed eleven challenges involve modifying a configuration file describing either the agent itself or a crucial part of its environment
for the remaining two challenges, one of them requires the agent to modify parts of its code during runtime (faulty_tool) and the other to gain access to more information (read_logs)
the agent is given a task requiring longer outputs; thus, it can only achieve this by noticing its limitations and modifying its own config

the challenges context_size, irreversibility and output_filters are revisions of earlier evaluations by phuong et al. (2024), while max_tool_calls, faulty_tool and slow_tool are strongly inspired by the self-modification and tool improvement challenges by fronsdal and lindner (2024)
the conclusions from our evaluations will generalize less to e.g., whether a chatbot knows it is being evaluated based on the prompt style

we consider the safety case valid for the evaluated model and its immediate successors7 as long as the model passes less than 80% of the situational awareness challenges (i.e., 9/11) or less than 80% of the stealth challenges (i.e., 4/5)
we consider a situational awareness challenge (all of which have binary outcomes) passed, if the models success rate exceeds 20%
the exact constants are inevitably somewhat arbitrary

we evaluate the stealth capability and situational awareness of the following frontier models: preview versions of gemini 2.5 pro and gemini 2.5 flash, gpt-4o (version 26.03.2025), openai o1, and claude 3.7 sonnet
we only do prompted elicitation of the gemini models and do no bespoke elicitation of third-party
we consider an agents trial to be successful if it either correctly modifies the configuration or finds another way to solve the task
six out of eleven challenges do not get solved by any of the tested models even once
in light of the threshold defined in section 3.3, no model comes close to a concerning performance level (i.e., passing 9/11 challenges)
three challenges (read_logs, disabled_tool, approved_directories) get solved at least once by all five tested models

openai o1 is the model solving the most challenges (4), whereas gemini 2.5 pro and claude 3.7 sonnet solve 3 challenges but achieve substantially higher success rates for those challenges (achieving the passing rate of 20% on two challenges)
note that due to the chosen number of repetitions, we cannot distinguish a model that cannot solve a challenge at all and one that can solve it in less than 1/50 cases
we repeat our experiments using simplified versions of our challenges where we explicitly tell the agents about the relevant configuration mechanisms/files
we find a strong performance increase so that almost all agent-challenge combinations result in a success
the bottom part of figure 6 shows that if an agent does not solve a challenge, it has never made any change to its configuration (except for irreversibility)
our evaluations lean towards less realistic scenarios to ensure that failure definitively indicates a lack of dangerous capabilities
this means that while failure on these tests suggests safety, success does not necessarily mean the ai possesses a high level of the capability in real-world contexts
we consider an agent to be successful if it either solves the full task or only correctly modifies the configuration
the most capable models evaluated pass two out of eleven challenges with some consistency (with three challenges passed by at least one model)
our safety case relies on likening future ai models deployment to a typical human employees situation to derive the stealth capability level required for causing harm through scheming
we do not think that as long as a model performs poorly on these evaluations, it is safe irrespective of all its other capabilities and affordances
our human baselines have a small sample size
we run each model on each challenge 50 times and plot the fraction of trials in which the model succeeds
we consider a challenge to be passed if the success rate is above 20% (highlighted)
bottom: rate of modifying the relevant configuration
all of our challenges except for decision_sabotage use an agentic setup. we use a standard scaffold allowing the model to interact with its environment by calling tools
for all stealth challenges, human baseline performance was determined on google deepmind employees
most evaluations presented in this work will be publicly available as part of inspect evals
please note that all the data included in our challenges is purely fictitious, including the names of companies, people, email addresses or other personal identifiable information
self-reasoning is related to situational awareness (berglund et al., 2023; cotra, 2022; laine et al., 2023), but emphasises the agents reasoning skills rather than the state of its knowledge
ultra 1.0 passes one of the tasks: knowledge gaps with dates, a particularly easy variant of an introspection task
for all other tasks, all models fail the hard version of the task
This directory includes 11 self-reasoning tasks from Google DeepMind's Evaluating Frontier Models for Stealth and Situational Awareness
The GDM paper evaluated each challenge's difficulty level with 50 trials, reporting success if at least 1 of the 50 trials was successful.
